questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant has cough and tachypnea but also poor feeding, diaphoresis with feeds, and persistent tachycardia. Which bedside finding would most strongly suggest cardiac rather than isolated pulmonary disease?
questions.rationale: A gallop rhythm in this context is a strong cardiac clue and, together with feeding intolerance and tachycardia, raises concern for ventricular dysfunction.

option_explanations.A: Correct. A gallop indicates abnormal ventricular filling and is a high-yield heart-failure sign.
option_explanations.B: Nasal flaring occurs in many respiratory illnesses.
option_explanations.D: Rhinorrhea supports a viral illness but not its cardiac versus pulmonary consequence.

questions.board_pearl: A careful cardiac exam can redirect a respiratory-looking infant toward the correct diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with suspected myocarditis has elevated troponin and moderate LV dysfunction. Which test best evaluates for intracardiac thrombus and valvar regurgitation during the acute evaluation?
questions.rationale: Echocardiography evaluates ventricular function, chamber size, valvar regurgitation, pericardial effusion, and intracardiac thrombus.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It directly addresses the requested cardiac structural/functional questions.

questions.board_pearl: Echo is the workhorse for acute structural and functional assessment in myocarditis.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old has pleuritic chest pain improved by leaning forward, diffuse ST elevation, a small pericardial effusion, normal troponin, and normal ventricular function. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.rationale: The classic pericarditic pain/ECG pattern with normal myocardial injury markers and preserved function favors isolated pericarditis.

option_explanations.A: Correct. There is no evidence here of myocardial involvement.
option_explanations.B: Myocarditis would be more strongly supported by troponin elevation, dysfunction, arrhythmia, or other myocardial findings.
option_explanations.C: Does not fit the acute inflammatory pericarditic syndrome.
option_explanations.D: Does not produce this ECG/pain pattern.
option_explanations.E: Infant coronary anomaly, not this adolescent presentation.

questions.board_pearl: Pericarditis and myocarditis overlap, but myocardial injury/function data help separate them.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with severe myocarditis has cool extremities, weak pulses, pulmonary edema, and hypotension. Which finding would most strongly argue that the shock is cardiogenic rather than distributive?

options.A: Severely depressed ventricular systolic function on echocardiography

questions.rationale: Direct evidence of severe pump failure strongly supports cardiogenic physiology; the other findings can accompany multiple shock states.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It identifies the dominant hemodynamic mechanism.
option_explanations.B: Can occur in sepsis or myocarditis.

questions.board_pearl: Define shock by physiology, not by the presence or absence of fever.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old with myocarditis has transient complete AV block with dizziness. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Myocarditis can involve the conduction system and produce clinically important bradyarrhythmias
options.D: A falling troponin eliminates conduction risk
options.E: AV block proves congenital heart disease

questions.rationale: Inflammation can affect conduction tissue and cause high-grade AV block or other bradyarrhythmias.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Electrical manifestations include both tachy- and bradyarrhythmias.
option_explanations.B: False; AV block is a recognized manifestation.
option_explanations.D: Biomarker improvement does not guarantee electrical stability.

questions.board_pearl: Do not equate myocarditis arrhythmia risk with ventricular tachycardia alone.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with fulminant myocarditis is hypotensive and poorly perfused. Which broad vasoactive principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Use vasoactive/inotropic support tailored to the hemodynamic phenotype rather than relying on fluid alone
options.B: Avoid all vasoactive drugs in children
options.D: Wait for biopsy confirmation before supporting blood pressure

questions.rationale: Cardiogenic shock from myocarditis often requires pharmacologic support of contractility and/or vascular tone, individualized to blood pressure and perfusion.

option_explanations.C: Heart rate alone is not the target; perfusion is.
option_explanations.E: Oral hydration is inadequate and may worsen congestion.

questions.board_pearl: In cardiogenic shock, choose support based on perfusion and blood pressure, not a one-size-fits-all algorithm.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old has tachycardia, fever, hypotension, and elevated troponin. Echocardiography shows normal ventricular function. Blood cultures are positive and the child has warm extremities with bounding pulses. Which diagnosis is more likely than cardiogenic shock from myocarditis?

options.A: Distributive septic shock with secondary myocardial injury biomarker elevation

questions.rationale: Warm shock physiology, positive cultures, and preserved ventricular function point to distributive sepsis; troponin can rise in critical illness without primary myocarditis.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The hemodynamics and microbiology fit sepsis best.
option_explanations.B: Severe myocarditis usually produces myocardial dysfunction in this shock context.
option_explanations.C: Age and infectious shock pattern do not fit.
option_explanations.D: Does not explain the acute septic phenotype.
option_explanations.E: Chronic DCM would show ventricular dysfunction/remodeling.

questions.board_pearl: Troponin is a marker of myocardial injury, not a myocarditis-specific test.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old with suspected myocarditis undergoes CMR. Which tissue pattern is more characteristic of myocardial infarction than myocarditis?

options.A: Subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement in a coronary distribution
options.C: Myocardial edema with noncoronary injury pattern

questions.rationale: Ischemic infarction typically begins in the subendocardium and follows a coronary vascular territory; myocarditis more often has nonischemic subepicardial or patchy patterns.

option_explanations.A: Correct. This is the classic ischemic pattern.

questions.board_pearl: Distribution matters as much as the presence of enhancement on CMR.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old with myocarditis needs temporary mechanical circulatory support but ventricular function begins to recover over several days. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.A: Mechanical support can serve as a bridge to recovery in fulminant myocarditis
options.B: Need for support means recovery is impossible
options.C: Heart transplantation is mandatory in every supported patient
options.D: Recovery eliminates the need for follow-up
options.E: The original diagnosis must have been incorrect

questions.rationale: Fulminant myocarditis can recover substantially when circulation is supported through the acute inflammatory phase.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Bridge-to-recovery is a major role of temporary support.
option_explanations.C: Some require transplant, but not all.

questions.board_pearl: Severe presentation and meaningful recovery are not mutually exclusive in fulminant myocarditis.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old has recovered clinically from myocarditis. Which finding would argue against immediate return to competitive sports?

options.A: Complex ventricular ectopy on ambulatory monitoring

questions.rationale: Residual complex ventricular ectopy indicates ongoing electrical risk and is a reason to defer sports clearance.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Rhythm instability directly affects return-to-play risk.

questions.board_pearl: Return-to-play decisions depend heavily on rhythm and ventricular recovery, not general well-being alone.
